\paragraph{The policy alone.} The policy without model inputs learned a
useful early search. In LOKO it reached 0.588 of the optimum after five
evaluations and 0.743 after ten, against 0.474 and 0.590 for TPE (differences
+0.115 [$-$0.006, +0.238] and +0.153 [$-$0.001, +0.305]), and it was
significantly better than TPE when trained on miniFE and tested on LULESH
(+0.177 [+0.039, +0.376] after ten evaluations). It did not beat the transfer
cost model, which reached 0.735 after five evaluations in LOKO, and the GP
caught up with it after ten. The policy was also inconsistent across kernels.
After ten evaluations it was the best method on the register-bound kernels
l844 (0.898) and l1080 (0.763), but it nearly failed on the reductions l1201
(0.147) and miniFE l290 (0.253), which need very few teams, because only
three training kernels are reductions.

\paragraph{The policy with model inputs.} The model inputs made the policy
more consistent. \code{rl\_hybrid} was significantly better than TPE in all
three folds after 1, 5, and 10 evaluations, for example +0.164 [+0.113,
+0.219] after five and +0.174 [+0.124, +0.232] after ten in LOKO, where it was
better on all 11 kernels. It was also significantly better than
\code{gp\_ei} after one and five evaluations in every fold (+0.123 [+0.073,
+0.172] after five in LOKO), because it does not start with random
configurations, although the GP overtook it after ten evaluations (LOKO
$-$0.048 [$-$0.153, +0.052]). Compared with the policy without model inputs,
it improved by only +0.049 after five evaluations in LOKO, which is not
significant. Its effect differed between kernels. The model inputs fixed the
reductions (after ten evaluations, l1201 rose from 0.147 to 0.619 and miniFE
l290 from 0.253 to 0.458), but the policy lost its advantage on the
register-bound kernels (l844 fell from 0.898 to 0.526 and l1080 from 0.763 to
0.353). The policy learned to follow the transfer model, and so inherited its
blind spots: the transfer model reached only 0.385 on l844 and 0.525 on l1080.

\paragraph{Against the transfer cost model.} Within the same applications
(LOKO), the transfer cost model remained significantly better than
\code{rl\_hybrid} after five evaluations ($-$0.098 [$-$0.178, $-$0.019]) and
ten evaluations ($-$0.071 [$-$0.140, $-$0.005]). Across applications, the
picture reverses. When trained on LULESH and tested on miniFE, the transfer
model reached only 0.627 after ten evaluations and 0.718 after 30, less than
random search, because the configurations that suit the LULESH kernels do not
suit the miniFE kernels. \code{rl\_hybrid} was significantly better (+0.142
[+0.010, +0.346] after five, +0.177 [+0.048, +0.399] after ten, and +0.206
[+0.026, +0.406] after 30 evaluations) and was the best method after five
evaluations (0.741, or 0.821 greedy). The policy learned when the transferred
predictions are worth following and how to fall back on the kernel's own
observations. Trained on miniFE and tested on LULESH, the two methods did not
differ significantly.

\paragraph{The fixed combination.} \code{gp\_transfer\_ei}, which combines
the same two models without learning, was erratic. It was the best method on
l1201 and miniFE l290, but after ten evaluations on miniFE l521 it had not
found any configuration faster than the baseline (share 0.000), against 0.951
for the transfer model alone. On that kernel the transfer model predicts a
gain of about 2.3\x{} for full-occupancy configurations with large blocks,
which suit the LULESH locality-bound kernels l649 and l1029, but all of these
configurations are slower than the baseline on miniFE l521. A GP fitted to
the residuals shifts all predictions by about the same amount, so the ranking
of candidates does not change, and EI keeps proposing configurations from the
same region. The learned policy avoided this failure (0.986), which shows
that learning how to weigh the two models matters more than having both.

\paragraph{Summary.} RL can learn a tuning policy that beats TPE and random
search in the first ten evaluations and, with the transfer and GP predictions
as inputs, does so consistently across folds. With 17 kernels, however, it
does not beat the simpler transfer cost model within the same applications,
and it costs about an hour of training per policy. The learned policy is
most useful when a new application is tuned with a model trained on another,
where the transfer model generalizes poorly. We therefore keep the transfer
model with EI in the tuner (Section~\ref{sec:combinedbatch}) and consider the
learned policy a candidate for transfer to new applications, which would need
many more training kernels to evaluate. These results are offline. The
landscapes have one batch timing per configuration, with a noise of about
1\%, and the discretized teams fractions do not include every configuration
that an online search could propose.

%=============================================================================
\section{Learned transfer with ranking and ensembles}
\label{sec:learnedtransfer}

The learned policy of Section~\ref{sec:rl} showed that the main weakness of
transferring knowledge across kernels is a wrong prior: the transfer cost model
predicts gains in regions that suit other kernels, and it generalized poorly
from LULESH to miniFE. We therefore tested three methods from the literature
that address this weakness more directly, on the same exhaustive landscapes,
folds, and score as Section~\ref{sec:rl}, and then evaluated the best one
online.

\subsection{Methods}
\begin{itemize}
\item \code{rgpe}, the \emph{ranking-weighted Gaussian process ensemble}
  (RGPE)~\cite{feurer2018rgpe}. It keeps one GP per training kernel, fitted
  to 300 random configurations of that kernel's landscape with the log
  speedup standardized per kernel, and one GP on the test kernel's own
  observations. Each model receives a weight equal to the fraction of 256
  posterior samples in which it has the fewest \emph{misranked pairs}, that
  is, pairs of observed configurations whose order the model predicts wrongly.
  The test kernel's own GP is scored with leave-one-out predictions, so that
  it cannot win by memorizing the observations. Training models whose median
  loss exceeds the 95th percentile of the own model's loss receive weight
  zero. The ensemble mean is the weighted sum of the models' means, its
  variance is the sum of the variances weighted by the squared weights, and
  the next configuration maximizes EI. Training kernels that rank the new
  kernel's observations badly thus lose their influence after a few
  evaluations. Before two observations, it follows the equally weighted mean
  of the training models.
\item \code{transfer\_rank}, a cost model trained with a \emph{pairwise
  ranking loss} instead of a regression loss, as in AutoTVM~\cite{chen2018autotvm}.
  A regression model predicts each configuration's log speedup, so kernels
  with large speedups (2.5\x{} on l649) dominate kernels with small ones
  (1.07\x{} on miniFE l210), although a tuner only needs the order of the
  configurations. We trained XGBoost~\cite{chen2016xgboost} with the
  \code{rank:pairwise} objective~\cite{burges2010ranknet}, which penalizes
  pairs of configurations of the same kernel that the model orders wrongly,
  with one group per training kernel and the configuration's percentile
  within its kernel (32 grades) as the relevance label. Eight models are
  trained on bootstrap samples of the training kernels. At every step each
  is fine-tuned with 20 additional trees on the test kernel's own
  observations, graded by their rank. The scores of each model are
  standardized, and the next configuration maximizes their mean plus their
  standard deviation over the eight models, an upper confidence bound in
  which the disagreement between models stands in for uncertainty. The
  features are those of the transfer cost model.
\item \code{wave\_blr}, a model of the launch configuration's \emph{wave}
  structure in the spirit of WaveTune~\cite{zhang2026wavetune}, which
  observed that kernel time is piecewise bilinear between wave boundaries. A
  \emph{wave} is one round of thread blocks that fills every SM, so the
  number of waves is the number of teams divided by the number of blocks that
  the GPU holds at once. We fitted Bayesian ridge regression on the kernel's
  own observations with a term per binary, the logarithms of the thread count
  and teams fraction and their product, the fill of the last wave, the
  occupancy, and for each wave bucket ($\lfloor \log_2 \text{waves}
  \rfloor$, clipped to $[-4, 6]$) an offset and slopes in the two
  logarithms. The first five configurations are \emph{anchors} spread over
  the wave buckets. It uses no other kernels.
\item \code{rank\_rgpe}, a hybrid: \code{transfer\_rank} for the first five
  proposals, then RGPE with the fine-tuned ranker as one more ensemble
  member (its standardized mean score and the spread of the eight models as
  uncertainty). \code{rank\_then\_rgpe} is the same without the ranker in the
  ensemble.
\end{itemize}

\subsection{Offline results}
Table~\ref{tab:learned} and Figure~\ref{fig:learned} show the share of the
optimum. The ranking model was the most consistent method. In LOKO it was the
best or tied for the best at every number of evaluations (0.641 after one,
0.908 after ten, and 0.981 after 30), significantly better than the learned
policy at every number of evaluations (+0.145 [+0.068, +0.234] after ten) and
than GP-EI after 1, 5, and 10. Its advantage over the regression transfer
model was +0.176 after one evaluation and +0.074 [$-$0.005, +0.172] after ten
in LOKO. Across applications, the regression model collapsed and the ranking
model did not. Trained on miniFE and tested on LULESH it was better by +0.211
[+0.036, +0.391] after ten evaluations, and trained on LULESH and tested on
miniFE by +0.209 [+0.006, +0.478] after 30. It found the optimum of l1080
quickly (0.856 after ten, against 0.525), a register-bound kernel that the
regression model and the learned policy had mispredicted.

RGPE started badly (0.172 after one evaluation in LOKO), because the equally
weighted mean of the training models is a weak prior. Once it had a few
observations, the weights moved to the models that rank the kernel correctly,
and the weight of the kernel's own GP rose from about 0.1 after three
evaluations to 0.3 to 0.56 after ten. It became the best method late in the
search in LOKO (0.885 after ten and 0.997 after 30, +0.038 [+0.011, +0.073]
over GP-EI after 30) and solved the reductions that every earlier method
struggled with (l1201 0.980 and miniFE l290 1.000 after ten evaluations).
From LULESH to miniFE, however, no LULESH model ranked the miniFE kernels
well, and RGPE reached only 0.554 after ten. The wave model beat TPE but not
GP-EI on the same kernel's observations, so the explicit wave structure did
not help at these budgets.

Neither hybrid was consistently better than the ranking model alone. After ten
evaluations, \code{rank\_rgpe} was slightly worse in LOKO ($-$0.025 [$-$0.091,
+0.023]) and slightly better from miniFE to LULESH (+0.026 [+0.008, +0.043]),
and \code{rank\_then\_rgpe} was much better from LULESH to miniFE (0.991,
+0.192 [+0.023, +0.440]) but much worse in the reverse direction ($-$0.110
[$-$0.185, $-$0.042]). Online, the per-kernel GPs of RGPE would also add about
70~s of fitting before the first batch. We therefore evaluated the ranking
model alone online.

\subsection{Online evaluation}
We added the ranking model to the tuner as \code{RankTransferSearcher} and
the strategy \code{rank-batch}. Like \code{combined-batch}
(Section~\ref{sec:combinedbatch}), it screens batches of 16 candidates with
batch replay, uses the measurements of the other kernels as training data
(leaving the tuned kernel out), and gives the two best screens the standard
measurement. It uses no portfolio and no prior, because the ranking model
already proposes good first batches. Ranker scores are not in units of
speedup, so the convergence stop of \code{combined-batch} cannot be used as
it is. We first used the largest EI of a GP fitted to the kernel's own screens,
computed from 32 screens on, with the same threshold of 0.002. We ran the
same five kernels with three seeds, a 300~s cap, and no cache, and re-measured
the shipped configurations of all compared methods together with the baseline
in the same five randomized rounds.

\code{rank-batch} shipped configurations as fast as \code{combined-batch}
(1.523\x{} against 1.521\x{}, ratio 1.001 [0.977, 1.021]) and reached good
configurations sooner. Its best screen reached 98\% of the best screen that
any run found on the kernel in 10 of 15 runs, against 7 for
\code{combined-batch}, and on l1201 it did so after a median of 8~s, while
\code{combined-batch} never did. However, its search took 168~s instead of
106~s, because the GP stop fired late and the 300~s cap ended 6 of 15 runs.
We therefore replayed simpler stop rules on the recorded traces. A
\emph{patience} rule, which stops after two consecutive batches that raise the
best screen by no more than 0.2\%, would have stopped \code{rank-batch} after
57~s on average and lost at most 0.6\% of its best screen. The same rule
would lose up to 2\% on the \code{combined-batch} traces and up to 17\% on the
\code{tpe-batch} traces, because TPE's early batches are poor and a pause in
progress does not mean that it has converged.

We then ran \code{rank-batch} with the patience stop online
(\code{rank-batch-patience}) and validated all four methods together in new
rounds. Table~\ref{tab:rankonline} shows the result. With the patience stop,
the ranking model shipped configurations as fast as \code{combined-batch}
(1.527\x{} against 1.528\x{}, ratio 0.999 [0.974, 1.020]) and
\code{tpe-batch} (ratio 0.995 [0.987, 1.004]), in 58~s of search instead of
106~s, and in 103~s inside the search function including two promotions
(176~s end to end, Section~\ref{sec:confirm}). The stop fired in all 15
runs, after 23~s to 131~s depending on the kernel. It was 2\% to 3\% better
than \code{combined-batch} on l649 and l1201 and 5\% worse on miniFE l290
(1.08\x{} against 1.14\x{}), where the speedups of the top screens differ by
about the batch measurement noise.

\subsection{Cheaper confirmation, several GPUs, and end-to-end time}
\label{sec:confirm}
After the patience stop, the two full measurements of the promoted
configurations took 45~s of the 103~s inside the search, and measuring the
baseline, classifying the kernel, and training the ranking models took about
another 70~s before the search began. Until now we reported times inside the
search function. Here we also report the end-to-end time of each run, from
the start of tuning a kernel to the shipped configuration, which includes
these steps. The end-to-end time of the original workflow, about 4000~s per
kernel, was measured the same way (Section~\ref{sec:endtoend}).

We made two changes to the tuner. The first is a cheaper \emph{batch
confirmation}. Instead of two full measurements, the three best screens are
re-timed with three interleaved repetitions each in one batch replay per
binary, next to the default configuration timed three times in batch mode on
the same GPU, and the tuner ships the configuration with the best speedup
over that default. Both sides of each speedup are therefore timed in the same
regime on the same GPU, which cancels the 1\% bias of batch timings on short
kernels (Section~\ref{sec:batch}). The second change uses several GPUs. Each
GPU replays in its own working directory, which links to the recording and
holds its own compiled image, and the replays run in forked processes, each
restricted to one GPU. Each batch of 16 candidates is dealt to the GPUs in
turn, and the timings of each GPU are scaled to those of the first GPU with a
factor from the default configuration timed in batch mode on every GPU (the
four T4 GPUs differed by at most 0.4\%). The baseline measurement and the
classification samples also run on three GPUs at once, but only the first
GPU's timings enter the baseline. We ran \code{rank-batch-patience} with batch
confirmation on one GPU (\code{rank-confirm}) and on four GPUs
(\code{rank-confirm-4gpu}) on the same five kernels with three seeds, and
re-measured the shipped configurations of all five strategies with the
baseline in the same five randomized rounds.

Table~\ref{tab:confirm} shows the result. The batch confirmation took 12~s
instead of 45~s and shipped configurations at least as fast as the full
measurements (ratio 1.003 [1.000, 1.007] over \code{rank-batch-patience}).
With it, a kernel took 140~s end to end on one GPU, against 176~s with full
measurements and 271~s for \code{combined-batch}, at the same quality (ratio
1.003 [0.976, 1.025] over \code{combined-batch}). Four GPUs reduced the end-to-end
time to 105~s, but only through the measurements before the search, which
fell from about 70~s to about 33~s. The search itself took 60~s on four GPUs
and 58~s on one. Splitting a batch of 16 among four replay processes saves
about 0.5~s per configuration, but every process pays the fixed cost of
loading the recording and warming up the GPU, and the per-GPU calibration
adds about 6~s, which cancels the saving. Several GPUs are more useful for
tuning different kernels at the same time, as our experiment drivers do, or
for screening a full batch on each GPU.

Against the original workflow, which took about 4000~s per kernel end to end
and shipped a true speedup of 1.39\x{}, the final tuner is about 29\x{}
faster on one GPU and 38\x{} faster on four, and it ships 1.53\x{}. Of the
105~s, about 33~s are spent before the search, 60~s in the search, and 12~s
in the confirmation.

\section{Discussion and recommendations}
\label{sec:discussion}

The answer to the first question is that knowledge of all metrics helps, but
only through metrics that vary with the launch configuration. DRAM traffic
and L2 hit rate explain the large gains on locality-bound kernels, registers,
spills, and occupancy explain the register-bound kernels, and SM and FP64
saturation of the baseline predicts when a kernel has nothing to gain.
Energy as now measured reveals real energy savings that a speed-only search
misses, and the global load and store request counts explain nothing. The
answer to the second question is that, once measurements are clean, the
choice among model-based search algorithms matters little, while the choice
of model features, initial design, budget, stopping rule, and above all the
cost of each evaluation matters more. Together, these changes made tuning
about 38\x{} faster end to end than the original workflow on four GPUs (29\x{}
on one) and improved the true speedup of the shipped configurations from
1.39\x{} to 1.53\x{} on the five kernels that we compared end to end
(Sections~\ref{sec:endtoend} and~\ref{sec:confirm}).

We recommend the following changes to the tuner, in order of expected
benefit per unit of effort.
\begin{enumerate}
\item Rank candidates with a cost model trained with a pairwise ranking loss
  across kernels, screen them in batches, and stop after two batches without
  gain (\code{rank-batch} with \code{patience}~2,
  Section~\ref{sec:learnedtransfer}), which ships the same configurations as
  the strategy of the next item in about half the search time. Confirm the
  three best screens in batch replay next to the default on the same GPU, and
  run the measurements before the search on several GPUs
  (Section~\ref{sec:confirm}).
\item Screen candidates with in-process batch replay (Section~\ref{sec:batch}),
  which made each screen about eight times cheaper, stop when the model's
  expected improvement falls below the measurement noise, and confirm the
  finalists with the standard measurement (Section~\ref{sec:combinedbatch}).
\item Keep the v3 measurement, including the metrics warm-up, the exclusivity
  guard, and validation of the shipped configuration against the baseline,
  with the default kept when the validated gain is below about 2\%.
\item Classify the kernel from warm baseline metrics, stop early on
  compute-saturated kernels, and choose the surrogate features by class.
\item Seed the search with a portfolio of configurations transferred from
  similar kernels, or rank candidates with a cost model transferred across
  kernels, instead of random initial samples (Section~\ref{sec:avenues}).
\item Screen candidates with a single short timing replay and fully measure
  only the best few, keeping the default configuration when a short kernel's
  promoted winner does not beat it, and reparameterize the launch bounds as a
  categorical binary class.
\item Use the best configurations of same-class kernels as a prior for the
  acquisition function, which kept the largest progress advantage in our
  tests.
\item Use MOTPE when energy matters, because it finds the time-energy
  trade-off at no cost in speed.
\end{enumerate}
A search policy learned with reinforcement learning is not yet worth adding
to the tuner, and neither is a ranking-weighted GP ensemble, which starts
slowly and needs per-kernel models. With 17 training kernels, it does not beat the transfer cost
model within the same applications, although it transfers better to a new
application (Section~\ref{sec:rl}).

\subsection{Limitations}
A limitation of this study is that it used one GPU model, the T4, which has a
low power limit and weak FP64 throughput, which affects both the bottleneck
classes and the time-energy trade-off. The applications were two proxy
applications with one recorded input each. The classification thresholds were
derived from the ten LULESH kernels, and miniFE is the only held-out test.
The offline estimates in Sections~\ref{sec:offline}, \ref{sec:targets},
and~\ref{sec:efficiency} use pools of configurations that earlier searches
chose, which bias them toward the regions those searches visited, and the
surrogate oracle used for the transfer estimates extrapolates beyond the
measured configurations. Repeated launches of one configuration in timing
mode reuse modified buffers, which can change the behavior of kernels that
update their inputs, although batch replay restores the inputs between
configurations. The learned policies were evaluated only offline, on
exhaustive landscapes with one batch timing per configuration and
discretized teams fractions, and were trained on 16 kernels or fewer.

\section{Reproducibility}
\label{sec:repro}

The code changes are on branch \code{measurement-v3} of the \code{openmp-rr}
repository: commit \code{a6a4418ce} (v3 measurement), commit \code{0d0b53d39}
(search strategies and the NVML device mapping fix), commit \code{5ee0f82bd}
(extended metrics, metric-aware search, early stopping), and commit
\code{865c4657b} (metrics warm-up and the adaptive pipeline). Each experiment directory
under \code{experiment-archives/} contains its scripts, logs, exit codes, and
a \code{RESULTS.md} file: \code{optimizer-study-2026-10-09}
(Section~\ref{sec:offline}), \code{measurement-fix-2026-10-09}
(Section~\ref{sec:measurement}), \code{search-study-2026-10-09}
(Section~\ref{sec:search}), \code{metric-search-2026-10-10}
(Sections~\ref{sec:metrics} and~\ref{sec:targets}),
\code{adaptive-2026-10-10} (Section~\ref{sec:adaptive}), and
\code{search-efficiency-2026-10-10} (Section~\ref{sec:efficiency}), and
\code{avenues-online-2026-10-11} (Section~\ref{sec:avenues}), and
\code{batch-replay-2026-10-11} (Section~\ref{sec:batch}). Batch replay is
commit \code{b6fd8c751}, and the combined strategy with the convergence stop is
commit \code{6f5c4c482} (\code{combined-batch-2026-10-12}, which also holds
the end-to-end comparison in \code{validate\_original.py},
\code{original-l*.json}, and \code{convergence\_vs\_original.log}).
The learned policies of Section~\ref{sec:rl} are in
\code{rl-tuning-2026-10-13}: \code{landscape.py} measured the exhaustive
landscapes (\code{landscape/*.csv}), \code{rl\_tune.py} and
\code{rl\_hybrid.py} run the offline comparison, and \code{analyze\_rl.py}
and \code{analyze\_hybrid.py} compute the summaries and confidence
intervals. PyTorch~2.4.1 (CPU) was installed in that directory's
\code{pylib}. Section~\ref{sec:learnedtransfer} is in
\code{learned-transfer-2026-10-13}: \code{learned\_transfer.py} and
\code{analyze.py} for the offline comparison, and \code{online/} for the
online runs (\code{analysis.log}, \code{analysis2.log},
\code{time\_to\_quality.log}, \code{patience\_stop*.log}). The tuner
changes are \code{RankTransferSearcher} in \code{RRUtil/Search.py} and the
\code{rank-batch}, \code{rank-rgpe-batch}, and \code{patience} options in
\code{RRUtil/Benchmark.py}. XGBoost~2.1.4 (\code{xgboost-cpu}) was installed
in that directory's \code{pylib}. The batch confirmation and the multi-GPU replays of
Section~\ref{sec:confirm} are commit \code{96aac7c74} (options \code{confirm}
and \code{devices} of \code{Kernel.Search}), with the runs in
\code{learned-transfer-2026-10-13/online/mgpu} (\code{orchestrate.sh},
\code{analyze\_mgpu.py}, \code{analysis.log}).
Optuna~3.6.1 is not part of the container, and the studies installed it in an
experiment-local directory on \code{PYTHONPATH}. Table~\ref{tab:env} lists the
environment variables that control the new behavior.
